I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over thirty years. I know what grows here and what sells. The soil is flat, the groundwater well is still working, and I can manage about twelve mu on my own now that my husband is older and the kids have gone to the city.

I'll do what I always do, what everyone on this street does: winter wheat on ten mu, then flip it to summer maize on the same ground after harvest. That rotation makes sense — the wheat goes in October, comes out in June, then immediately plant maize. Two crops, same field, one year. I've done this my whole life. The grain station still buys both, so I know I'll have cash.

For wheat I'll use an improved variety — 济麦22 or whatever the county seed shop has in stock. I won't try something new I don't know. I'll do three irrigations: once before sowing to wet the bed, once at jointing, once at heading. Four would be better but the water costs money and the village committee keeps warning us about the aquifer. I rotary-till after maize harvest to chop the stubble under.

For maize I go hybrid, direct seeded into the stubble, no tillage. My neighbor showed me this five years ago and I kept doing it — saves fuel and the yield is the same. One irrigation at silking if it's dry. Usually the summer rains handle it.

I also keep two mu of vegetables by the house edge — garlic, cabbage, some beans — mostly for ourselves and to sell at the Thursday market. This I do by feel, no big plan.

I put fertilizer on heavy because that's how I was taught. I know the agronomist at the township says to use less but I don't want a bad harvest.
